# Prerequisites {#sec-prerequisites}

This chapter gets your computer ready for the rest of the book. By the end you will
have installed Julia and an editor, downloaded the book's data and exercises, and
run a first script that draws a plot.

Follow the steps in order. Where they differ between operating systems, pick your
system's tab. Plan for about an hour the first time — most of it is waiting while
packages install — and keep an internet connection until @sec-instantiate is done.
If a step does not behave as described, see @sec-troubleshooting.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will install

| What | Why |
|---|---|
| **Julia** (through `juliaup`) | the language itself |
| **VS Code** and its Julia extension | where you write and run code |
| **The book folder** | data, exercises and the list of packages the book uses |
| **The book's packages** | data frames, plots and models, at the exact versions the book was built with |

You do not need git, R or Quarto.
:::

## Step 1: open a terminal {#sec-terminal}

A terminal is a window where you type commands instead of clicking. You need it only
for installing Julia; after that, everything happens inside VS Code.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Windows

Open the Start menu, type **PowerShell** and open *Windows PowerShell* (or
*Terminal*, on Windows 11).

## macOS

Press `Cmd+Space`, type **Terminal** and press `Return`.

## Linux

Press `Ctrl+Alt+T` on most distributions, or look for *Terminal* in the applications
menu.
:::

To run a command, paste it into the terminal and press `Enter`. Pasting is `Ctrl+V`
on Windows, `Cmd+V` on macOS and `Ctrl+Shift+V` in most Linux terminals.

## Step 2: install Julia {#sec-installing}

Use **`juliaup`**, the official installer and version manager. Do not install Julia
through a system package manager (`apt`, `brew`), which tends to ship outdated
versions.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Windows

```powershell
winget install --name Julia --id 9NJNWW8PVKMN -e -s msstore
```

If Windows asks you to accept the Microsoft Store terms, type `Y` and press `Enter`.

## macOS and Linux

```bash
curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh
```

The installer asks whether to proceed with the default settings. Press `Enter` to
accept them.
:::

When it finishes, **close the terminal and open a new one** — the `julia` command only
becomes available in new terminals. Then check the installation:

```bash
julia --version
```

It should print something like `julia version 1.12.6`. Any version from 1.10 upwards
works with this book. Now type `julia` and press `Enter` to start Julia itself. The
prompt changes to `julia>`; type `1 + 1`, press `Enter`, and Julia answers `2`. Leave
with `exit()`.

Later, `juliaup update` upgrades Julia and `juliaup status` lists the installed
versions.

## Step 3: download the book folder {#sec-download}

The book comes with a folder that holds the example data, the exercise checker and
the list of packages the book needs.

1. Go to <https://github.com/esantos2ua/EcologicalAnalysesInJulia>.
2. Click the green **Code** button, then **Download ZIP**.
3. Unzip the file:

   ::: {.panel-tabset}
   ## Windows

   Right-click the downloaded file and choose **Extract All…**. Work in the extracted
   folder, not inside the ZIP: files opened from inside a ZIP are read-only copies.

   ## macOS

   Double-click the downloaded file.

   ## Linux

   Right-click the file and choose *Extract Here*, or run `unzip` on it.
   :::

4. Move the extracted folder, `EcologicalAnalysesInJulia-main`, somewhere permanent
   such as your *Documents* folder. You can rename it, but avoid putting it inside
   *Downloads*, which some systems clean up automatically.

Inside you should see, among others, the folders `data` and `exercises` and the files
`Project.toml` and `Manifest.toml`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## If you already use git

Clone the repository instead of downloading the ZIP; `git pull` then brings in updates
to the book:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/esantos2ua/EcologicalAnalysesInJulia.git
```
:::

## Step 4: install VS Code {#sec-editor}

**VS Code** with the official Julia extension is the standard editor for Julia: it
offers an integrated REPL (the console where code runs), a variable browser, a plot
pane, a debugger and line-by-line evaluation — the functional equivalent of RStudio.

1. **Install VS Code** from <https://code.visualstudio.com> and open it.
2. **Install the Julia extension.** Open the Extensions panel (`Ctrl+Shift+X`;
   `Cmd+Shift+X` on macOS), search for *Julia* and install the extension published
   by *julialang*. It finds the Julia installed by `juliaup` on its own.

If you prefer a fully open-source build, [VSCodium](https://vscodium.com) is VS Code
compiled from the same MIT-licensed source without Microsoft's telemetry, and installs
the same Julia extension from the [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org) registry.
[Antigravity](https://antigravity.google), another editor derived from VS Code, also
runs the same extension. Everything in this book applies to all three. Other options are **Pluto.jl** (reactive notebooks,
excellent for teaching) and any editor with LSP support through `LanguageServer.jl`.

## Step 5: open the book folder {#sec-vscode-setup}

1. **Open a folder, not a file.** In VS Code, use *File → Open Folder…* and choose the
   book folder from @sec-download. If VS Code asks whether you trust the authors of
   the files, answer yes. The folder you open determines both where Julia looks for
   files and which packages it uses.
2. **Check the environment.** The status bar at the bottom of the window should read
   `Julia env:` followed by the name of the book folder. If it shows something like
   `Julia env: v1.12` instead, click that entry and choose the book folder.
3. **Start the REPL.** Open the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`; `Cmd+Shift+P` on
   macOS) and run *Julia: Start REPL*, or press `Alt+J` then `Alt+O`. A panel opens at
   the bottom with the `julia>` prompt, already inside the book folder and its
   environment.

::: {.r-equivalent}
**In R**

Opening a folder in VS Code plays the role of opening an `.Rproj` in RStudio: it sets
the working directory. Unlike RStudio, it also selects the package environment
(@sec-environments), so the right package versions come along automatically.
:::

## Step 6: install the book's packages {#sec-instantiate}

Click in the REPL panel and run:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.instantiate()
```

This reads `Manifest.toml`, downloads every package the book uses at the exact
version listed there, and compiles them.

::: {.callout-warning}
## This takes a while

The first time, `Pkg.instantiate()` can take from several minutes to half an hour,
depending on your computer and connection. Plotting and modelling packages are large,
and Julia compiles them ahead of time so they run fast later. Progress lines keep
appearing while it works; let it finish and do not close VS Code. You only do this
once per computer.
:::

## Step 7: check that everything works {#sec-setup-check}

The book folder includes a checker that you will also use for the exercises from
@sec-julia-basics on. Load it and ask it to check your setup:

```julia
include("exercises/check.jl")
check("setup")
```

If everything is in place you will see:

```
✓ Julia 1.12.6
✓ Working folder is the book folder
✓ Book environment is active
✓ Data file found: data/ponds.csv
✓ All 19 packages installed
Ready. Continue with the first script.
```

A line with ✗ says what is wrong and how to fix it; @sec-troubleshooting has more
detail.

## Step 8: a first script {#sec-first-script}

With the book folder open and the REPL running, create a file called `first-steps.jl`
in the folder root (*File → New File*, or `Alt+J` then `Alt+N`) and paste:

```julia
## Load packages
using CSV, DataFrames, CairoMakie

## Where am I?
pwd()               # the folder you opened
readdir("data")     # files inside data/

## Read the example data
ponds = CSV.read(joinpath("data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame)
first(ponds, 5)
describe(ponds)

## Plot richness against pond area
fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Pond area (m²)", ylabel = "Species richness",
          xscale = log10)
scatter!(ax, ponds.area_m2, ponds.richness)
fig
```

Lines starting with `##` split the script into **cells**. Put the cursor in the first
cell and press `Alt+Enter` to run it, then keep going cell by cell
(`Alt+Shift+Enter` runs the cell and jumps to the next one). A few things to notice:

- **Loading packages is slow the first time** in each session — that is the
  compilation latency discussed in @sec-latency. Later cells run immediately.
- **Paths are relative to the folder you opened.** `pwd()` confirms it, which is why
  `joinpath("data", "ponds.csv")` works without typing the full path. `joinpath`
  inserts the right separator on every operating system.
- **`describe` is your first data check.** It shows that `canopy` has 7 missing
  values and that `area_m2` is strongly right-skewed (median around 149 m², maximum
  near 2000 m²) — which is why the plot uses a log scale.

The shortcuts you will use constantly:

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Shift+Enter` | run the current line or selection, then move to the next |
| `Ctrl+Enter` | run the current line or selection, staying put |
| `Alt+Enter` | run the current cell (a block delimited by `##` lines) |
| `Alt+J`, `Alt+R` | restart the REPL |
| `Ctrl+C` in the REPL | interrupt a running computation |

On macOS, `Alt` is the Option key; `Ctrl` stays `Ctrl`. Shortcuts and menu names were
checked against version 1.249 of the Julia extension in September 2026.

**Inspecting the environment.** Click the Julia icon in the Activity Bar (the
left-hand strip). The **Workspace** panel lists every variable in the session —
`ponds`, `fig`, `ax` — with its type and size; expand an entry to look inside. For a
data frame, hover over its name and click the *Open in VS Code* icon, or run
`vscodedisplay(ponds)` in the REPL, to open it in a spreadsheet-like grid — the
equivalent of RStudio's `View()`.

**Plots.** Evaluating `fig` opens the figure in the **plot pane**, a VS Code tab. The
**Plot Navigator** panel, below the Workspace, keeps the history of the session's
plots; with the plot pane focused, the arrow keys move through it. To save a figure
to disk, use `save("richness-area.png", fig)`.

## Troubleshooting {#sec-troubleshooting}

**`julia` is not recognized / `command not found`.**
: Close every terminal and open a new one; the installer only updates new terminals.
  If it still fails, run the installation command of @sec-installing again.

**Windows: `winget` is not recognized.**
: `winget` comes with the *App Installer* app. Update *App Installer* from the
  Microsoft Store, or search for **Julia** in the Microsoft Store and install it from
  there — it is the same `juliaup` installer.

**Linux: `curl: command not found`.**
: Install `curl` with your distribution's package manager (for example
  `sudo apt install curl` on Ubuntu), then repeat @sec-installing.

**VS Code says it cannot find Julia.**
: In a terminal, run `where.exe julia` (Windows) or `which julia` (macOS, Linux) and
  copy the path it prints. In VS Code, open the settings (`Ctrl+,`; `Cmd+,` on macOS),
  search for `julia.executablePath` and paste the path there. Then restart VS Code.

**The status bar shows `Julia env: v1.12` (or another version) instead of the book folder.**
: VS Code has the wrong folder open, or a single file. Use *File → Open Folder…* and
  choose the book folder itself — the one containing `Project.toml` — not a folder
  above or inside it. Then restart the REPL (`Alt+J`, `Alt+R`).

**`include("exercises/check.jl")` fails with `No such file or directory`.**
: The REPL is not running in the book folder. `pwd()` shows where it is. Open the
  book folder as above and restart the REPL.

**`Pkg.instantiate()` seems frozen.**
: It is probably compiling; this is the slow part. As long as new lines keep
  appearing every few minutes, wait. If it stopped with an error — for example
  because the connection dropped — run `Pkg.instantiate()` again; it picks up where it
  left off.

**`Package CairoMakie not found in current path` (or another package).**
: Either the book environment is not active (check the status bar) or
  @sec-instantiate has not finished. `check("setup")` tells you which.

**The first `using CairoMakie` in each session takes a minute.**
: That is normal: Julia compiles code the first time it runs in a session
  (@sec-latency). Later commands are fast.

## Under the hood: project environments {#sec-environments}

You have already used an environment without having to think about it: that is what
the status bar in @sec-vscode-setup shows. This section explains what it is — the
concept that differs most from common practice in R.

In R, `install.packages()` installs into a global library shared by all your projects.
In Julia, each project has its own environment, described by two files:

- **`Project.toml`** — the direct dependencies you declared.
- **`Manifest.toml`** — the full resolved dependency tree, with exact versions of
  everything.

Together they make an analysis reproducible by construction: anyone who has your
project folder and runs `Pkg.instantiate()` gets exactly your versions — which is
what you did in @sec-instantiate.

::: {.r-equivalent}
**In R**

`Project.toml` + `Manifest.toml` play the role of `renv.lock`, but they are part of the
language rather than an add-on package. Activating an environment is the default
operation, not the exception.
:::

`Pkg.status()` lists the packages in the active environment:

::: {#env-status .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
using Pkg
Pkg.status()
```

## Under the hood: Quarto {#sec-quarto}

You do not need this section to follow the book. It is for readers who want to build
the book themselves or write documents like it.

This book is written in [Quarto](https://quarto.org), the direct successor to
`bookdown`. Since version 1.5, Quarto executes Julia blocks natively, without going
through Jupyter.

````markdown
```{{julia}}
#| label: example
1 + 1
```
````

The repository's `README.md` explains how to render the book.

## Challenges {.unnumbered}

1. In the REPL, press `]` to enter package mode (the prompt turns blue; `Backspace`
   leaves it). Run `activate my-test` and then `add DataFrames`: this creates an
   environment in a new folder, `my-test`. Inspect the `Project.toml` it generated,
   then run `activate .` to return to the book's environment.
2. Delete `my-test/Manifest.toml`, activate `my-test` again and run `resolve`. What
   changes?
3. Run `first-steps.jl` (@sec-first-script) cell by cell. In the Workspace panel,
   which types did `CSV.jl` assign to the `region` and `canopy` columns, and why is
   the type of `canopy` different from that of `area_m2`?
